lines: An order moves through four states in just a few seconds. New, then paid, then shipped, then refunded.
A poll watching that row runs on its own schedule, samples it once, and happens to catch it at refunded.
Every record anyone can query later says this order went straight to refunded. There's no trace it was ever paid, or ever shipped, at all.
Here's the question before I show you what actually catches the states a poll misses.
The identical four-second sequence, but this time a trigger copies every change into a separate shadow table the instant each one happens, inside the same transaction as the real write.
Does that shadow table see the states the poll walked straight past?
answer: Saying no sounds reasonable if you think of a trigger as watching the transaction as a whole, the way a poll effectively does.
But a trigger fires on every individual statement, each one inside its own transaction. Four separate updates to the same row trigger four separate captures, not one.

lines: Here's why a poll behaves this way at all.
A poll is one query, asked on a timer. Whatever happens to a row between two consecutive runs of that timer is simply invisible to it.
It isn't a bug. The poll was never watching continuously. It was only ever sampling.
I ran that exact sequence against this sandbox's own real database, not a simulation.
A single poll query against the test order sees exactly one state, the one it happened to catch.
A real logical replication slot, reading the identical window, hands back all four states, new, paid, shipped, refunded, in the exact order they actually happened.
Here's a second, completely different way a poll goes wrong.
A row gets inserted and deleted inside the same short window. A poll that asks what's changed since the last watermark finds nothing at all.
Not because nothing happened. Because the one thing that would prove something happened is no longer there to be found.
I ran that exact insert-then-delete against the real database.
The poll's own watermark query comes back with zero rows for that order, identical to what it would show if that order had simply never existed.
The replication slot, reading the same window, shows exactly one delete event, naming the row and the moment it happened.
A trigger fixes the gaps a poll has. It doesn't do that for free.
The trigger runs inside the same transaction as the write it's capturing, copying the change into a shadow table before that transaction even commits.
Which means every single write to the real table is now, mechanically, two writes instead of one.
I measured that doubling directly, and then measured what the log costs for the identical information.
Four real writes to a test order produce exactly four rows in the trigger's own shadow table. Not three, not five. One for one.
The replication slot gets the identical four changes for nothing extra, because it's just reading what the server had already written to its own log for recovery.
Step back, and three approaches to the same problem come out with three very different bills.
Polling misses whatever happens between its own samples. A trigger sees everything, but doubles every write along the way. The log sees everything too, and costs nothing extra to read.
That last part sounds like it can't possibly be the whole story, and it isn't.
Here's the part reading the log doesn't let you skip.
The log itself costs nothing extra to read. What does holding a position in it, so you can keep reading from where you left off, actually cost?
answer: Saying there's no extra cost treats the read as the whole story, but a consumer that wants to resume later has to hold a place in that log somehow.
That place is a real, ongoing cost: it pins storage on the source for as long as you haven't caught up, needs real privileges to set up, and breaks outright if a failover loses it.
